title: Lean catheter pathway across four hospitals: catheter days and catheter-associated infections
subtitle: Lean project with staggered starts on 12 wards in Hospitals A to D
statement: Indwelling urinary catheters stay in longer than needed on 12 medical and surgical wards across four hospitals: 19 percent of ward patients had a catheter at the last point count and 38 of 120 reviewed catheters had no documented indication. The project will use value stream mapping and standard work (nurse-driven removal, a daily huddle check and a flowsheet reminder) to shorten catheter duration, measured in a way that separates real change from noise across hospitals that start at different times.
whoAffected: Adult inpatients on 12 wards, especially older men after surgery and patients catheterised in emergency or theatres; ward nurses who own removal; physicians and theatre teams who insert catheters; the four ward manager champions.
whatHurts: Unneeded catheters cause infections, bacteraemia, discomfort, delirium and immobility; two catheter-source bacteraemias occurred last year. Nurses are unsure whether they may remove catheters without an order.
currentPractice: Removal depends on a physician order; indications are often undocumented; catheter days are recorded in flowsheets in three hospitals and on paper in Hospital D.
whyNow: Council approval is in place, a Lean coach is available for one hospital at a time, and the point count showed a high share of catheters without an indication.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients have a urinary catheter only while it is needed, and no patient has a catheter reinserted because it was removed without a plan.
summary: Problem framed as a multi-site Lean project on catheter duration, with infections as a descriptive safety outcome.
